blocks.p: For a square matrix $A$, an eigenvector is a nonzero vector $v$ that $A$ only stretches or shrinks along its own line: multiplying by $A$ is the same as multiplying by a number $\lambda$, the eigenvalue:
Since $v \ne 0$, this has a solution only when $A-\lambda I$ is singular, which gives the characteristic equation:
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
For $\lambda=1$: $(A-I)v=0$ gives $v_1+v_2=0$, so $v = \begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}$. For $\lambda=3$: $(A-3I)v=0$ gives $v_1=v_2$, so $v = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$.

**Check by substitution:** $A\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}$ and $A\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\3\end{bmatrix}$. **Check by trace and determinant:** $1+3 = 4 = 2+2$ and $1\times3 = 3 = 4-1$.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $B = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

For $\lambda=5$: $-v_1+v_2=0$, so $v = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$. For $\lambda=2$: $2v_1+v_2=0$, so $v = \begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}$. Checks: $2+5 = 7 = \text{trace}(B)$ and $2\times5 = 10 = \det B$.

blocks.p: For a triangular (or diagonal) matrix the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 2, 3 and −1. A real symmetric matrix always has real eigenvalues.

list: **Writing $\det(A) - \lambda = 0$.** Subtract $\lambda$ from every diagonal entry first, then take the determinant.
**Accepting $v = 0$ as an eigenvector.** Eigenvectors are nonzero by definition; any nonzero multiple of a valid one also works.
**Skipping the checks.** The sum of eigenvalues must equal the trace and their product the determinant. If either fails, the characteristic equation has a slip.
**Assuming eigenvalues of $A+B$ are sums of eigenvalues.** That holds for $A+kI$, not for two general matrices.

exam.note: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are listed under Linear Algebra in the GATE 2027 syllabi for CS, EC, EE, IN and ME (the EC syllabus writes 'eigen values and eigen vectors').
